member.name: TuningOverrides
member.para: What it took to make the constants settable at all (2026-08-20). C# inlines a const at every use site, so nothing can override one at run time; the exposed constants had to become static fields. Converting all 97 of 's with a script and building came back with zero warnings, which is the measurement that made this feasible rather than merely plausible - the tree had been checked first for the things that genuinely require a compile-time constant, and has none of them: no constant patterns, no attribute arguments, no stackalloc, no cross-class const references.

Three traps the conversion surfaced, all of which had to be fixed rather than reasoned around. First, nine of 's constants are derived from others, and static field initializers run in declaration order - is declared 23 lines before , so as a plain field it would have initialized to -5.0 instead of 25.0, silently. They are expression-bodied properties now, which fixes the order and also makes an override of an input reach everything downstream of it. (The ninth was missed by the first script pass because its initializer sits on the following line - grep for the declaration, not for the assignment.) Second, used as a default parameter value, which must be a compile-time constant; the parameter is nullable now. Third, one test declared a const from two tuning values.

The whole 1653-test suite passing after the conversion is what says the derived-as-properties approach yields the right numbers: several fixtures assert on positions computed from exactly those derived values.

Why the snapshot exists. These are process-global statics. The CLI parses one command line and exits, so it would never notice; the test suite parses hundreds in one process, and without restoring the compiled-in values first, the first test to use --set: would change the meaning of every test after it. Restoring on every also makes parsing the same command line twice give the same answer, which is a property worth having regardless.
